claim: PARP-7 is a critical regulator of the innate immune response.
source: PARP-7 is a critical regulator of the innate immune response.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about PARP-7's role.

claim: The protein targets of PARP-7 mono-ADP-ribosylation (MARylation) are largely unknown.
source: What remains unclear is the mechanism by which PARP-7 regulates this process, namely because the protein targets of PARP-7 mono-ADP-ribosylation (MARylation) are largely unknown.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in current knowledge about PARP-7 targets.

claim: PARP-13 is a major target of PARP-7.
source: We found that the inactive PARP family member, PARP-13—a critical regulator of the antiviral innate immune response—is a major target of PARP-7.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: PARP-13 is preferentially MARylated on cysteine residues in its RNA binding zinc finger domain.
source: PARP-13 is preferentially MARylated on cysteine residues in its RNA binding zinc finger domain.
evidence: This is a key finding from the study's site mapping experiments.

claim: Cysteine is a major MARylation acceptor of PARP-7 across the proteome.
source: Proteome-wide ADP-ribosylation analysis reveals cysteine as a major MARylation acceptor of PARP-7.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from proteome-wide analysis.

claim: Most PARP family members catalyze mono-ADP-ribosylation (MARylation).
source: Most PARP family members catalyze the transfer of a single unit of ADP-ribose from nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) to amino acids on protein targets, a reversible post-translational modification (PTM) known as mono-ADP-ribosylation (MARylation) (Daugherty et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Knockout of PARP-7 enhances nucleic acid sensor agonist- or virus-induced interferon-beta (IFN-β) expression in various cell types.
source: Knockout of PARP-7 enhances nucleic acid sensor agonist- or virus-induced interferon-beta (IFN-β) expression in various cell types (Yamada et al., 2016; Kozaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Viral titers after infection with several single-strand RNA viruses are lower in PARP-7 knockout or knockdown cells compared to wild-type cells.
source: Consistent with this notion, viral titers after infection with several single-strand RNA viruses, including influenza, vesicular stomatitis virus, encephalomyocarditis virus, and mouse hepatitis virus (a murine coronavirus), are lower in PARP-7 knockout or knockdown cells compared to wild-type cells (Yamada et al., 2016; Grunewald et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PARP-7 facilitates viral replication, in part, by shutting down IFN-β production.
source: These results show that PARP-7 facilitates viral replication, in part, by shutting down IFN-β production.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies showing lower viral titers in PARP-7 knockout cells.

claim: Glutamate, aspartate, and arginine are historically considered major ADPr acceptor residues.
source: Historically, the chemical nature of the amino acid-MAR bonds in proteins was examined by chemical stability studies (Payne et al., 1985; Cervantes-Laurean et al., 1993; Hsia et al., 1985; Krantz and Lee, 1976; McDonald and Moss, 1994). This led to the notion that the major ADPr acceptor residues are the acidic amino acids, glutamate (Glu) and aspartate (Asp), as well as the basic amino acid arginine (Arg).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical chemical stability studies.

claim: Serine, tyrosine, histidine, and cysteine can act as ADPr acceptors in addition to glutamate, aspartate, and arginine.
source: More recently, however, mass spectrometry-based proteomics has revealed that in addition to Glu/Asp and Arg, serine (Ser), tyrosine (Tyr), histidine (His), and cysteine (Cys) can also act as ADPr acceptors (Buch-larsen, 2020; Larsen et al., 2018; Leslie Pedrioli et al., 2018; Palazzo et al., 2018; Leidecker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent mass spectrometry studies.

claim: 5-Bn-2-e-NAD+ is a much better substrate for IG-PARP-7 compared to 5-Bn-6-a-NAD+.
source: Compared to 5-Bn-6-a-NAD+, we found that 5-Bn-2-e-NAD+ is a much better substrate for GFP-IG-PARP-7 as evidenced by the greater labeling (biotin signal following click conjugation to biotin-azide) of GFP-tagged IG-PARP-7 (GFP-IG-PARP-7) (auto-MARylation) as well as the labeling of many other discrete bands (trans-MARylation) in HEK 293 T cell lysates (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: 5-Bn-2-e-NAD+ is not a substrate for GFP-WT-PARP-7.
source: Importantly, we did not detect labeling of GFP-WT-PARP-7, indicating that 5-Bn-2-e-NAD+ is not a substrate for GFP-WT-PARP-7 (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: A total of 250 direct targets of PARP-7 were identified using the chemical genetic approach.
source: We identified a total of 250 direct targets of PARP-7, many of which are RNA binding and RNA regulatory proteins (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from LC-MS/MS analysis.

claim: Many PARP-7 targets are RNA binding and RNA regulatory proteins.
source: We identified a total of 250 direct targets of PARP-7, many of which are RNA binding and RNA regulatory proteins (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the proteomics data analysis.

claim: A total of 189 interacting proteins of PARP-7 were identified using BioID proximity labeling.
source: We identified a total of 189 interacting proteins of PARP-7 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from BioID-LC-MS/MS analysis.

claim: A subset of PARP-7 interactors overlap with targets identified using the chemical genetic approach.
source: We found that a subset of these PARP-7 interactors overlapped with targets identified using our CG approach (Figure 2a), suggesting that these interactors could be intracellular MARylation targets of PARP-7.
evidence: This is shown in the Venn diagram in Figure 2a.

claim: Gene ontology analysis of PARP-7 targets shows significant enrichment of terms related to viral processes, RNA regulation, and the innate immune response.
source: We found a significant enrichment of terms related to viral processes, RNA regulation, and the innate immune response (Figure 2b, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The enrichment of viral processes, RNA regulation, and innate immune response terms is consistent with the known role of PARP-7 in regulating the innate immune response during viral infection.
source: The enrichment of these terms is consistent with the known role of PARP-7 in the regulation of the innate immune response during viral infection (Yamada et al., 2016; Kozaki et al., 2017; Grunewald et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the GO analysis results to previous literature.

claim: PARP-13 exists as two major isoforms: PARP-13.1 (ZAPL) and PARP-13.2 (ZAPS).
source: PARP-13 is unique among PARP family members for two main reasons: i. it exists as two major isoforms, the full-length protein known as PARP-13.1 (ZAPL) and a truncated variant known as PARP-13.2 (ZAPS) that is devoid of the catalytic domain
evidence: This is established knowledge about PARP-13 structure.

claim: PARP-13.1 is catalytically inactive despite having the catalytic domain.
source: ii. despite having the catalytic domain, PARP-13.1 is catalytically inactive.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PARP-13.1 function.

claim: PARP-13.2 is induced by interferons and viral infection.
source: PARP-13.1 is constitutively expressed in most cells and PARP-13.2 is induced by interferons (e.g. IFN-β) as well as viral infection (Schwerk et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PARP-13.1 is the major isoform in HEK 293 T cells.
source: In HEK 293 T cells, PARP-13.1 and PARP-13.2 are expressed, but PARP-13.1 is the major isoform (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PARP-13.1 is the major endogenous isoform that interacts with Myc-BirA*-PARP-7 in HEK 293 T cells.
source: Indeed, we confirmed that PARP-13.1 is the major endogenous isoform that interacts with Myc-BirA*-PARP-7 in HEK 293 T cells (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Both PARP-13.1 and PARP-13.2 are MARylated by GFP-PARP-7 in cells.
source: We found that both PARP-13.1 and PARP-13.2 are MARylated by GFP-PARP-7 (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: In the absence of PARP-7, MARylation of PARP-13.1 or PARP-13.2 is not detected.
source: In the absence of PARP-7, we do not detect MARylation of PARP-13.1 or PARP-13.2 (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Phthal01 is most potent against PARP-7 with an IC50 of 14 nM.
source: We found that Phthal01 is most potent against PARP-7 (IC50 = 14 nM), followed closely by PARP1 (IC50 = 21 nM), and PARP2 (IC50 = 28 nM) (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from in vitro inhibitor profiling assays.

claim: Phthal01 is at least 13-fold selective for PARP-7 versus other PARP family members besides PARP-1 and PARP-2.
source: Phthal01 is at least 13-fold selective for PARP-7 versus the other PARP family members besides PARP-1 and PARP-2 (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from in vitro inhibitor profiling assays.

claim: Phthal01 dose dependently inhibits auto-MARylation of PARP-7 in GFP-PARP-7 expressing HEK 293 T cells with an EC50 of approximately 60 nM.
source: We found that Phthal01 dose dependently inhibits auto-MARylation of PARP-7 in GFP-PARP-7 expressing HEK 293 T cells (EC50 ~60 nM) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Phthal01 at 1 μM completely inhibits both auto-MARylation of PARP-7 and PARP-7-mediated trans-MARylation of PARP-13.2.
source: Phthal01 (1 μM), but not the PARP1/2-selective inhibitor veliparib (1 μM), completely inhibits both auto-MARylation of PARP-7 and PARP-7-mediated trans-MARylation of PARP-13.2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1f.

claim: The catalytic activity of PARP-7 is required for PARP-13.2 MARylation in cells.
source: Taken together, these results show that the that catalytic activity of PARP-7 is required for PARP-13.2 MARylation in cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Phthal01 inhibition experiments.

claim: GST-PARP-7 trans-MARylates His6-SUMO-PARP-13.2 in vitro in a time-dependent manner.
source: In the presence of a physiological concentration of NAD+ (100 μM), GST-PARP-7 trans-MARylated His6-SUMO-PARP-13.2 in addition to itself (auto-MARylation) in a time-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: His6-SUMO-PARP-10 poorly trans-MARylates His6-SUMO-PARP-13.2 in vitro despite strong auto-MARylation.
source: Despite strong auto-MARylation, His6-SUMO-PARP-10 poorly trans-MARylated His6-SUMO-PARP-13.2 under similar conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The interaction between PARP-7 and PARP-13.2 is independent of PARP-7 catalytic activity.
source: GST-PARP-7 co-immunoprecipitated with His6-SUMO-PARP-13.2 under all conditions, demonstrating that the interaction between PARP-7 and PARP-13.2 is independent of PARP-7 catalytic activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments under different conditions including with and without NAD+ and with Phthal01.

claim: HgCl2 reduces substantially (~90%) the ADPr signal on HA-PARP-13.2 in lysates from HEK 293 T cells expressing GFP-PARP-7.
source: In lysates from HEK 293 T cells expressing GFP-PARP-7 and HA-tagged PARP-13.2, we found that HgCl2 (2 mM) reduces substantially (~90%) the ADPr signal on HA-PARP-13.2, whereas neutral NH2OH (0.4 M) only partially reduces (~30%) this signal (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by chemical stability experiments shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Neutral NH2OH only partially reduces (~30%) the ADPr signal on HA-PARP-13.2 in lysates from HEK 293 T cells expressing GFP-PARP-7.
source: In lysates from HEK 293 T cells expressing GFP-PARP-7 and HA-tagged PARP-13.2, we found that HgCl2 (2 mM) reduces substantially (~90%) the ADPr signal on HA-PARP-13.2, whereas neutral NH2OH (0.4 M) only partially reduces (~30%) this signal (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by chemical stability experiments shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Neutral NH2OH reduces substantially (~90%) the ADPr-signal on PARP-10 in lysates from HEK 293 T cells expressing GFP-PARP-10.
source: In contrast, in lysates from HEK 293 T cells expressing GFP-PARP-10 and HA-tagged PARP-13.2, we found that neutral NH2OH reduces substantially (~90%) the ADPr-signal on PARP-10 whereas HgCl2 has no effect (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by chemical stability experiments shown in Figure 4b.

claim: HgCl2 has no effect on the ADPr-signal on PARP-10 in lysates from HEK 293 T cells expressing GFP-PARP-10.
source: In contrast, in lysates from HEK 293 T cells expressing GFP-PARP-10 and HA-tagged PARP-13.2, we found that neutral NH2OH reduces substantially (~90%) the ADPr-signal on PARP-10 whereas HgCl2 has no effect (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by chemical stability experiments shown in Figure 4b.

claim: PARP-10 is auto-MARylated predominately on Glu/Asp.
source: The latter result is consistent with previous studies from our lab and others showing that PARP-10 is auto-MARylated predominately on Glu/Asp (Morgan and Cohen, 2015; Kleine et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Trans-MARylation of PARP-13.2 by PARP-10 was not detected when these two constructs were co-expressed.
source: Despite the strong auto-MARylation activity of PARP-10 in cells, we did not detect trans-MARylation of PARP-13.2 when these two constructs were co-expressed (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Treatment with either neutral NH2OH or HgCl2 equally reduces PARP-7 auto-MARylation.
source: Treatment with either neutral NH2OH or HgCl2 equally reduces PARP-7 auto-MARylation suggesting it may be modified on both cysteine and acidic residues (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by chemical stability experiments shown in Figure 4b.

claim: PARP-7 may be auto-MARylated on both cysteine and acidic residues.
source: Treatment with either neutral NH2OH or HgCl2 equally reduces PARP-7 auto-MARylation suggesting it may be modified on both cysteine and acidic residues (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is inferred from the chemical stability experiments showing equal reduction by both treatments.

claim: PARP-13.2 is a selective target of PARP-7 that is MARylated predominately on Cys residues.
source: Taken together, these results show PARP-13.2 is a selective target of PARP-7 that it is MARylated predominately on Cys residues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chemical stability studies.

claim: MacroD2 efficiently reverses auto-MARylation of PARP-10.
source: We found that while macroD2 efficiently reverses auto-MARylation of PARP-10, macroD2 only partially reverses both auto-MARylation of PARP-7 and trans-MARylation of PARP-13.2 (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by enzymatic removal experiments shown in Figure 4c.

claim: MacroD2 only partially reverses both auto-MARylation of PARP-7 and trans-MARylation of PARP-13.2.
source: We found that while macroD2 efficiently reverses auto-MARylation of PARP-10, macroD2 only partially reverses both auto-MARylation of PARP-7 and trans-MARylation of PARP-13.2 (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by enzymatic removal experiments shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The half-life (t1/2) of ADPr in PARP-10 is 15 min.
source: We found that the half-life (t1/2) of ADPr in PARP-10 is 15 min whereas the t1/2 of ADPr in PARP-13.2 is 189 min (Figure 4d–f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from time course experiments shown in Figure 4d-f.

claim: The half-life (t1/2) of ADPr in PARP-13.2 is 189 min.
source: We found that the half-life (t1/2) of ADPr in PARP-10 is 15 min whereas the t1/2 of ADPr in PARP-13.2 is 189 min (Figure 4d–f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from time course experiments shown in Figure 4d-f.

claim: The Cys-ADPr bond is more stable in HEK 293 T cells than the Glu/Asp-ADPr bond.
source: The longer t1/2 of MARylated PARP-13.2 versus MARylated PARP-10 suggests that the Cys-ADPr bond is more stable in HEK 293 T cells than the Glu/Asp-ADPr bond.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in half-lives measured in the time course experiments.

claim: No change in the Cys- or Glu/Asp-ADPr signal was observed over time (up to 24 hr) in denatured lysates.
source: We observed no change in the Cys- or Glu/Asp-ADPr signal over time (up to 24 hr) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by chemical stability experiments in denatured conditions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Cys-ADPr is more stable than Glu/Asp-ADPr in HEK 293 T cells due to enzymatic rather than chemical differences.
source: We observed no change in the Cys- or Glu/Asp-ADPr signal over time (up to 24 hr) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a). This result shows that Cys-ADPr is more stable than Glu/Asp-ADPr in HEK 293 T cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both bonds are chemically stable when denatured, but have different half-lives in cells.

claim: Phthal01 increased the protein levels of ectopically expressed GFP-PARP-7 and MycX2-PARP-13.2.
source: The HEK 293 T cell time course experiments revealed that Phthal01 increased the protein levels of ectopically expressed GFP-PARP-7 and MycX2-PARP-13.2 (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the time course experiments shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endogenous PARP-7 protein levels increase substantially upon treatment with Phthal01.
source: We found that endogenous PARP-7 protein levels increase substantially upon treatment with Phthal01; however, the levels of endogenous PARP-13.1 did not change (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in A549 cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c.

claim: The levels of endogenous PARP-13.1 did not change upon treatment with Phthal01.
source: We found that endogenous PARP-7 protein levels increase substantially upon treatment with Phthal01; however, the levels of endogenous PARP-13.1 did not change (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in A549 cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Endogenous PARP-7 levels are regulated by its catalytic activity.
source: These results suggest that while endogenous PARP-7 levels are regulated by its catalytic activity, endogenous PARP-13.1 levels are not regulated by PARP-7 catalytic activity under these conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Phthal01 increases PARP-7 but not PARP-13.1 levels.

claim: Endogenous PARP-13.1 levels are not regulated by PARP-7 catalytic activity under basal conditions.
source: These results suggest that while endogenous PARP-7 levels are regulated by its catalytic activity, endogenous PARP-13.1 levels are not regulated by PARP-7 catalytic activity under these conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Phthal01 does not change PARP-13.1 levels.

claim: A total of 1712 ADPr sites with a localization probability of >90% were identified across all three experimental conditions.
source: We identified a total of 1712 ADPr sites with a localization probability of >90% in all three conditions (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the EThcD MS analysis.

claim: Amino acid-ADPr sites were identified on all known ADPr acceptor residues, including Cys, Glu, Asp, His, Lys, Arg, Ser, Thr, and Tyr.
source: We identified amino acid-ADPr sites on all known ADPr acceptor residues, including Cys, Glu, Asp, His, Lys, Arg, Ser, Thr, and Tyr (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the EThcD MS analysis.

claim: In the GFP-PARP-7 alone condition, endogenous PARP-13 is MARylated exclusively on Cys residues.
source: In the GFP-PARP-7 alone condition, endogenous PARP-13 (likely representing the two major isoforms PARP-13.1 and PARP-13.2) is MARylated exclusively on Cys residues (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplements 3–4, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EThcD MS analysis shown in Figure 5a and supplementary figures.

claim: Seven Cys-ADPr sites were identified in endogenous PARP-13.
source: Intriguingly, all but one of the seven identified Cys-ADPr sites in endogenous PARP-13 are located in the four N-terminal zinc-finger (ZnF 1–4) domains; one Cys-ADPr (Cys721) is located in the inactive, catalytic domain of PARP-13.1 (Figure 5b,c, Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the EThcD MS analysis.

claim: All but one of the seven identified Cys-ADPr sites in endogenous PARP-13 are located in the four N-terminal zinc-finger (ZnF 1–4) domains.
source: Intriguingly, all but one of the seven identified Cys-ADPr sites in endogenous PARP-13 are located in the four N-terminal zinc-finger (ZnF 1–4) domains; one Cys-ADPr (Cys721) is located in the inactive, catalytic domain of PARP-13.1 (Figure 5b,c, Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EThcD MS analysis and shown in Figure 5b,c.

claim: One Cys-ADPr (Cys721) is located in the inactive, catalytic domain of PARP-13.1.
source: Intriguingly, all but one of the seven identified Cys-ADPr sites in endogenous PARP-13 are located in the four N-terminal zinc-finger (ZnF 1–4) domains; one Cys-ADPr (Cys721) is located in the inactive, catalytic domain of PARP-13.1 (Figure 5b,c, Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EThcD MS analysis and shown in Figure 5b,c.

claim: Five out of the six ZnF Cys-ADPr sites are Zn-coordinating Cys residues.
source: Five out of the six ZnF Cys-ADPr sites are Zn-coordinating Cys residues (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure visualization in Figure 5c.

claim: All of the endogenous PARP-13 Cys-ADPr sites in the ZnF domains are conserved between human, mouse, and rat.
source: Despite the relatively low conservation of PARP-13 across species, all of the endogenous PARP-13 Cys-ADPr sites in the ZnF domains are conserved between human, mouse, and rat (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence alignment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: When PARP-13.2 was co-expressed with PARP-7, additional Cys-ADPr sites in the ZnF in PARP-13 were identified.
source: When PARP-13.2 was co-expressed with PARP-7, we identified additional Cys-ADPr sites in the ZnF in PARP-13.
evidence: This is a result from the EThcD MS analysis comparing different conditions.

claim: In the PARP-7 and PARP-13.2 co-expression condition, other amino acid-ADPr sites are identified, most prominently on Arg and Tyr, but with intensities at least an order of magnitude lower than Cys-ADPr.
source: In this condition, other amino acid-ADPr sites are identified, most prominently on Arg and Tyr; however, the intensities for Arg-ADPr and Tyr-ADPr are at least an order of magnitude lower than the intensities found for Cys-ADPr (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the EThcD MS analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Cys MARylation in PARP-13.2 is dependent on the co-expression of PARP-7.
source: Cys MARylation in PARP-13.2 is dependent on the co-expression of PARP-7 since we only detect Ser-ADPr (three sites) and Arg-ADPr (one site) in the PARP-13.2 alone condition (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the EThcD MS results across different conditions shown in Figure 5a.

claim: In the PARP-13.2 alone condition, only Ser-ADPr (three sites) and Arg-ADPr (one site) are detected.
source: Cys MARylation in PARP-13.2 is dependent on the co-expression of PARP-7 since we only detect Ser-ADPr (three sites) and Arg-ADPr (one site) in the PARP-13.2 alone condition (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the EThcD MS analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: GFP-PARP-7 is auto-MARylated predominately on Cys residues.
source: In addition to identifying Cys-ADPr sites in PARP-13, we also found that GFP-PARP-7 is auto-MARylated predominately on Cys residues (Figure 5—figure supplement 6, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EThcD MS analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: Cys39 in PARP-7 was identified as an auto-MARylation site in a previous MS method using standard HCD fragmentation.
source: One Cys, Cys39, was identified in a previous MS method using standard HCD fragmentation (Gomez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Two Cys-ADPr sites (Cys543 and Cys552) reside in the catalytic domain of PARP-7.
source: Two Cys-ADPr sites (Cys543 and Cys552) reside in the catalytic domain of PARP-7.
evidence: This is a result from the EThcD MS analysis.

claim: At much lower intensities, several Tyr-ADPr, His-ADPr, and Arg-ADPr sites were found in PARP-7.
source: At much lower intensities, we found several Tyr-ADPr, His-ADPr, and Arg-ADPr sites in PARP-7 (Figure 5—figure supplement 6, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the EThcD MS analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: The major auto-MARylation sites in PARP-7 are Cys residues.
source: Regardless, it is clear that the major auto-MARylation sites in PARP-7 are Cys residues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EThcD MS analysis showing predominant Cys-ADPr sites.

claim: Mutation of all of the Cys residues to alanine residues in the ZnF domains of PARP-13.2 (CtoA ZnF all) substantially reduces PARP-13.2 MARylation compared to WT PARP-13.2.
source: In HEK 293 T cells expressing both GFP-PARP-7 and MycX2-PARP-13.2, we found that mutation of all of the Cys residues to alanine (Ala) residues in the ZnF domains of PARP-13.2 (CtoA ZnF all) substantially reduces PARP-13.2 MARylation compared to WT PARP-13.2 (Figure 5d, Figure 5—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Mutation of the Cys residues to Ala residues in either ZnF domains 1–2 (CtoA ZnF 1–2) or 3–4 (CtoA ZnF 3–4) modestly reduces PARP-13.2 MARylation.
source: Mutation of the Cys residues to Ala residues in either ZnF domains 1–2 (CtoA ZnF 1–2) or 3–4 (CtoA ZnF 3–4) modestly reduces PARP-13.2 MARylation (Figure 5d, Figure 5—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The reduction in PARP-7-mediated MARylation of PARP-13.2 in the Cys mutants is not due to a loss in the interaction between PARP-13 and PARP-7.
source: The reduction in PARP-7-mediated MARylation of PARP-13.2 in the Cys mutants is not due to a loss in the interaction between PARP-13 and PARP-7 as shown by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 8.

claim: The primary sites of MARylation by PARP-7 on PARP-13.2 are the ZnF Cys residues.
source: Together these data support that the primary sites of MARylation by PARP-7 on PARP-13.2 are the ZnF Cys residues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis and MS data.

claim: A total of 939 unique amino acid-ADPr sites on a total of 490 proteins were identified as putative PARP-7 targets.
source: Using the above criteria, we identified a total of 939 unique amino acid-ADPr sites on a total of 490 proteins (Figure 6a) as putative PARP-7 targets.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the proteome-wide EThcD MS analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Of the 939 putative PARP-7 target sites, the majority (471 Cys-ADPr sites on 374 proteins) were on Cys residues.
source: Of these sites, the majority (471 Cys-ADPr sites on 374 proteins) were on Cys residues (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the proteome-wide EThcD MS analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: 48 proteins overlap between the PARP-7-targeted, Cys-ADPr modified proteins and the direct PARP-7 targets identified using the chemical genetic strategy.
source: When we compared the PARP-7-targeted, Cys-ADPr modified proteins to the direct PARP-7 targets identified using our CG strategy, we found 48 overlapping protein targets (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is shown in the Venn diagram in Figure 6b.

claim: PARP-13 was a top target among the 48 overlapping proteins between Cys-ADPr modified proteins and chemical genetic targets.
source: Among these 48 overlapping proteins, PARP-13 was a top target.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the two datasets.

claim: The vast majority of PARP-7 target proteins are MARylated on a single Cys.
source: We found that the vast majority of proteins are MARylated on a single Cys (Figure 6d and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown in the distribution graph in Figure 6d.

claim: PARP-13, with 11 sites identified, stands out as the only target with >4 Cys-ADPr sites.
source: Intriguingly, PARP-13, with 11 sites identified, stands out as the only target with >4 Cys-ADPr sites (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is shown in the distribution graph in Figure 6d.

claim: There is a preference for a proline (Pro), followed by an Arg, in the +2 position relative to Cys-ADPr sites.
source: While we did not observe a strong preference for a particular amino acid at the −1 position, we did find a preference for a proline (Pro), followed by an Arg, in the +two position (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is shown in the IceLogo analysis in Figure 6c.

claim: The proximal sequence surrounding the Cys-ADPr site is not a strong determinant for MARylation targeting by PARP-7.
source: This analysis suggests that the proximal sequence surrounding the Cys-ADPr site is not a strong determinant for MARylation targeting by PARP-7.
evidence: This is inferred from the IceLogo analysis showing weak sequence preferences.

claim: 5-Bn-2-e-NAD+ is a better substrate for floor position engineered PARP-12, I660G PARP-12 (IG-PARP-12) compared to 5-Bn-6-a-NAD+.
source: Similarly, we found that 5-Bn-2-e-NAD+ is a better substrate for floor position engineered PARP-12, I660G PARP-12 (IG-PARP-12) compared to 5-Bn-6-a-NAD+ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: PARP-13.1 and PARP-13.2 have distinct roles in innate antiviral immune response.
source: Recent studies show that PARP-13.1 and PARP-13.2 have distinct roles in innate antiviral immune response: PARP-13.2 binds and degrades host mRNAs (e.g. IFN-β), thereby negatively regulating the interferon response, whereas PARP-13.1 targets viral RNA and is the major antiviral effector (Schwerk et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: PARP-13.2 binds and degrades host mRNAs (e.g. IFN-β), thereby negatively regulating the interferon response.
source: Recent studies show that PARP-13.1 and PARP-13.2 have distinct roles in innate antiviral immune response: PARP-13.2 binds and degrades host mRNAs (e.g. IFN-β), thereby negatively regulating the interferon response, whereas PARP-13.1 targets viral RNA and is the major antiviral effector (Schwerk et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: PARP-13.1 targets viral RNA and is the major antiviral effector.
source: Recent studies show that PARP-13.1 and PARP-13.2 have distinct roles in innate antiviral immune response: PARP-13.2 binds and degrades host mRNAs (e.g. IFN-β), thereby negatively regulating the interferon response, whereas PARP-13.1 targets viral RNA and is the major antiviral effector (Schwerk et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: The ZnF domains of PARP-13.1 and PARP-13.2 are required for binding to both host and viral mRNAs.
source: The ZnF domains of PARP-13.1 and PARP-13.2 are required for binding to both host and viral mRNAs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PARP-13 function.

claim: MARylation of Cys residues in the ZnF domains may alter or disrupt RNA binding by PARP-13.
source: Since the Cys residues in the ZnF domains of PARP-13 are important for Zn2+ coordination, it is possible that MARylation of these Cys residues alters or disrupts RNA binding.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the structural role of Cys residues in ZnF domains.

claim: PARP-13.2 stimulates the interferon response in response to influenza A viral infection via direct activation of the cytosolic nucleic acid sensor RNA helicase RIG-I.
source: PARP-13.2 stimulates the interferon response in response to influenza A viral infection via direct activation of the cytosolic nucleic acid sensor RNA helicase RIG-I (Hayakawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: PARP-13.2 interacts with RIG-I and stimulates its oligomerization and ATPase activity, leading to interferon induction.
source: PARP-13.2 interacts with RIG-I and stimulates its oligomerization and ATPase activity, leading to interferon induction.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PARP-13.2 function.

claim: The interaction between PARP-13.2 and RIG-I is dependent on the ZnF domains of PARP-13.2.
source: This interaction is dependent on the ZnF domains of PARP-13.2, hence Cys MARylation of PARP-13.2 by PARP-7 could potentially disrupt the interaction between PARP-13.2 and RIG-I.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, with a speculative inference about the effect of MARylation.

claim: Cys MARylation of PARP-13.2 by PARP-7 could potentially disrupt the interaction between PARP-13.2 and RIG-I.
source: This interaction is dependent on the ZnF domains of PARP-13.2, hence Cys MARylation of PARP-13.2 by PARP-7 could potentially disrupt the interaction between PARP-13.2 and RIG-I.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the location of MARylation sites.

claim: PARP14 MARylates PARP-13 on several Glu/Asp residues in the C-terminus of the protein.
source: In a previous chemical genetic study, we found that PARP14 MARylates PARP-13 on several Glu/Asp residues in the C-terminus of the protein (Carter-O'Connell et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: PARP-13.1 and PARP-13.2 can be poly-ADP-ribosylated (PARylated) in response to cell stress.
source: Another study showed that PARP-13.1 and PARP-13.2 can be poly-ADP-ribosylated (PARylated) in response to cell stress, although the PARP that mediates PARylation of PARP-13.1/2 was not identified (Leung et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: PARylation of PARP-13 could be catalyzed by PARP1/2.
source: Serines are known sites of PARylation by PARP1 and PARP2 (Larsen et al., 2018; Palazzo et al., 2018); therefore, PARylation of PARP-13 could be catalyzed by PARP1/2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of Ser-ADPr sites in PARP-13.2 and citations showing PARP1/2 PARylate serines.

claim: Trans-M/PARylation of PARP-13 by other PARP family members suggests that PARP-13 is an important integrator of active PARP signaling.
source: Trans-M/PARylation of PARP-13 by other PARP family members suggests that PARP-13 is an important integrator of active PARP signaling.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that multiple PARPs modify PARP-13.

claim: M/PARylation at distinct amino acid acceptors may elicit different downstream effects.
source: An intriguing idea is that M/PARylation at distinct amino acid acceptors elicits different downstream effects.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative hypothesis.

claim: Cys MARylation was originally described for the bacterial ADP-ribosyltransferase Pertussis toxin (PTX).
source: Cys MARylation was originally described for the bacterial ADP-ribosyltransferase Pertussis toxin (PTX) (Mangmool and Kurose, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PTX MARylates a Cys in the carboxyl terminus of the alpha submit of the G proteins, Gi and Go.
source: PTX MARylates a Cys in the carboxyl terminus of the alpha submit of the G proteins, Gi and Go (Mangmool and Kurose, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Studies dating back 30 years ago described endogenous Cys MARylation, similar to PTX-dependent MARylation, but the enzyme(s) that catalyzes Cys MARylation were not identified.
source: Studies dating back 30 years ago described endogenous Cys MARylation, similar to PTX-dependent MARylation (Jacobson et al., 1990; Tanuma, 1988) but the enzyme(s) that catalyzes Cys MARylation were not identified.
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical studies.

claim: This study provides strong evidence that PARP-7 catalyzes Cys MARylation.
source: In this study, we provide strong evidence that PARP-7 catalyzes Cys MARylation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: Previous studies showed that PARP-7 auto-MARylates predominately on a Cys residue (Cys39).
source: Our results are consistent with previous studies showing that PARP-7 auto-MARylates predominately on a Cys residue (Cys39) (Gomez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: HPF1 can act as an auxiliary factor to influence amino acid target preference for PARP1/2.
source: Recent studies on the amino acid selectivity of PARP1/2-mediated PARylation provides some clues: for example, a recent crystal structure of the histone PARylation factor (HPF1) (Gibbs-Seymour et al., 2016)—PARP2 complex shows that HPF1 interacts directly with the NAD+-binding site of PARP2 (Suskiewicz et al., 2020), and demonstrates that HPF1 can act as an auxiliary factor to influence amino acid target preference.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent structural and functional studies.

claim: In the absence of HPF1, PARP1 predominately PARylates on Glu/Asp residues.
source: In the absence of HPF1, PARP1 predominately PARylates on Glu/Asp residues; however, in the presence of HPF1, PARP1 predominately PARylates on Ser residues (Palazzo et al., 2018; Eisemann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the presence of HPF1, PARP1 predominately PARylates on Ser residues.
source: In the absence of HPF1, PARP1 predominately PARylates on Glu/Asp residues; however, in the presence of HPF1, PARP1 predominately PARylates on Ser residues (Palazzo et al., 2018; Eisemann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PARP-7 may have auxiliary factors that influence its amino acid target preference, similar to HPF1 for PARP1.
source: Perhaps this is similarly the case for PARP-7, and future studies may focus on identifying potential auxiliary factors for PARP-7.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the HPF1-PARP1 example.

claim: A catalytically inactive PARP-7 mutant is expressed at higher levels than WT-PARP-7.
source: This is consistent with previous studies showing that a catalytically inactive PARP-7 mutant is expressed at higher levels than WT-PARP-7 (Gomez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: There is a first PARP-7 inhibitor (RBN-2397) in Phase I clinical trials for solid tumor cancers.
source: Currently, there is the first PARP-7 inhibitor (RBN-2397) in Phase I clinical trials for solid tumor cancers (NCT04053673).
evidence: This is stated as current information with a clinical trial identifier.

claim: RBN-2397 represents the first clinical trial for an inhibitor of a MARylating PARP.
source: This is the first clinical trial for an inhibitor of a MARylating PARP and represents and exciting new direction in the PARP field.
evidence: This is stated as a significant development in the field.
